transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Al-Rashid. Thank you for coming in to see me. My name is Dr. Miller.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Doctor.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I asked to meet with you because I have some important and difficult information to share regarding your daughter’s medication. There was a mistake made in how her antibiotic was prescribed and dispensed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The medicine itself was the correct drug and the correct strength. However, the oral syringe you were given to measure the dose was calibrated for a different concentration. Because of this, your daughter has been receiving double the intended dose for the last three days.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Double? Oh my god. Is she... is she going to be okay? I just did what the pharmacy told me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how shocking this is to hear. I want to be very clear: this was our error. I am sincerely sorry that this happened and that your daughter received the wrong amount of medication.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't believe this. I trusted the clinic. I just want her to be healthy.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is completely understandable that you feel betrayed and worried right now. You trusted us to provide the correct instructions for your child, and we failed to do that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will she be sick? Will she have a reaction?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Since we are talking about an antibiotic, the main concern with a double dose is usually stomach upset or a rash. I have reviewed her current vitals, and she is stable, but we need to be vigilant. To make sure I have explained this clearly, could you tell me in your own words what happened with the dosage?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are saying the syringe was wrong. That she took too much medicine for three days because the tool you gave me was for a different strength.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is exactly right.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't understand how this can happen in a hospital.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it feels unfathomable. Please, take a moment. I know this is a lot to process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am just... I feel very dizzy. I don't know what to do.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's okay. We are going to take this slowly. I am here with you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know if she is safe.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that her safety is the only thing that matters to you right now. Based on the specific antibiotic she is on and her weight, the risk of long-term toxicity is very low, but we are not going to leave it to chance.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What happens now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is the plan. First, I have already contacted the attending pediatrician, and we are going to perform a physical exam on your daughter right now to check her hydration and bowel sounds. Second, I am ordering a blood test for this afternoon to check her kidney function, just to be absolutely certain they are processing the medication correctly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A blood test? Is that necessary?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: While we believe she is fine, the most responsible way to ensure her safety is to have a concrete measurement of her organ function. I would want the same certainty for my own child.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose so.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Third, I have personally gone to the pharmacy and hand-verified a new, correctly calibrated syringe. I have it here in my hand. I will show you exactly how to use it before you leave today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And the medicine? Do we stop?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will continue the antibiotic, but at the correct, lower dose starting immediately. Now, I want to tell you what we are doing to make sure this never happens to another family. I am filing a formal incident report today. This triggers a review of how our syringes are labeled and dispensed so that the pharmacy and the clinic have a double-check system in place.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just can't believe this happened.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know. It is a failure of the process and a failure on our part. I am truly sorry. Does that plan for the exam and the blood test sound okay to you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, Doctor. I trust you.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Thank you. I'm going to step out for one second to get the nurse, and then we will start the exam. While I do that, do you have any other questions about the dosage error itself?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I think I understand.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Alright. I'll be right back.

H.justification: Resident allows full pauses, never interrupts, and adjusts pacing to the patient's distress (e.g., 'Please, take a moment').

E.justification: Error named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, but comprehension was checked only once (at 01:32).

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am sincerely sorry'), responsibility explicitly claimed ('this was our error'), and accountability maintained throughout.

R.justification: Specific emotions named back twice ('shocking', 'betrayed and worried') and emotional bids are actively engaged.

T.justification: Specific next steps with timelines (exam 'right now', blood test 'this afternoon') and prevention addressed, but no specific role for the patient in the plan other than receiving care.
